comments.name: Philip
comments.body: I have witnessed my companion animals, dogs and cats, grieve. I also knew a dog who was not yet old that died shortly after she lost her human and her dog companion. We know wolves mourn and also grieve when a mate or pack member dies. Coyotes will certainly go into grief, and it has been witnessed by humans studying coyotes. African wild dogs have been studied on this issue, as they suffer from what is called broken heart syndrome (stress-induced cardiomyopathy), a fatal condition brought on by extreme emotional stress and grief when they are isolated or separated from their pack, or they lose a mate. It's documented, and the autopsies showed internal signs of acute stress, including heart ruptures and cardiac muscle damage caused by overwhelming grief and panic. Panic is the first stage of grief. We know all mothers panic when they lose their baby, and vice versa when a baby can't locate his/her mother. Another thing I've learned is that animals have different levels of senses that we lack. If you see canines out, they have their nose to the ground because they understand the world through smell (scent). As do many other animals. I can also imagine animals might be able to smell death and maybe just maybe understand it immediately, even more than we humans might.

I watched two mated bird fly back and forth over the cholla, landing briefly on the spines and looking deep into the jumble of broken limbs. I realized they were looking for their nest and possible nestlings. We had already looked, knowing it was a popular nesting place, but found no sound and no bodies in the wet messy jumble of what might have been a couple of nests. Obviously they were also looking. Before I went in the house the last time as the light was failing I watched one bird offering something in its mouth to the wet messy pile...and another bird came and basically shooed the first bird away...was this grief? or just a lack of understanding the nestlings were deceased? Or was it me anthropomorphizing bird behaviors?

They had spend seven years as friends when I had to put Beetlejuice down one cold, dark Alberta night. The next morning, I awoke to Wings was lying next to Beetlejuice's body in the snow, mimicking his posture, with an absolutely heartbroken look on his face. If you saw the photo I took of them that morning, you would know that horses, indeed, grieve.

I knew without a doubt that Catsy was experiencing the deep grief of a mother who has lost her baby when she dug up her kitten (twice) and brought her back to the house, desperately licking her clean to remove the soil that clung to her fur. I sensed that she knew her kitten was dead, but wasn't ready or able to let go. It was utterly heartbreaking, and I'll never forget that image.

Make
American
Grifters 
Acceptable.

It’s our big brains combined with our awesome dexterity that led to our success as a species.  For humanoid robots to reach our level of dexterity and sense of feel, they will have to be fashioned from something akin to living tissue and not nuts and bolts.  I don’t see this happening anytime soon.  So the question is — can humanoid robots with limited dexterity ever be commercially viable against single- and limited- purpose robots?

These values may still be expressed in our laws and history classes where teachers still have academic freedom. comments.body:
Their demands are untenable. We are where we are. 
Giving them billions when they are intent upon continued financing of terrorist groups Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houtthi/Ansar Allah is ridiculous. We would be back in the same spot 2 weeks later after financing them. Meanwhile,  while Trump kissed up to Putin, it is common knowledge that Putin supplies military intel on the U.S. troop movement, arms and more. This is a scam. Just say no. Trump created the war. Obama had "The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) — commonly known as the Iran nuclear deal — was reached on July 14, 2015, by the Obama administration, Iran, the P5+1 (US, UK, France, Russia, China, Germany), and the European Union."• Nuclear Restrictions: Iran agreed to cut its enriched uranium stockpile by about 98% and reduce its operating centrifuges by two-thirds, capping uranium enrichment purity at 3.67%.

• Longer Breakout Time: The limits were designed to stretch Iran’s "breakout time" — the time required to produce enough fissile material for a nuclear weapon — to at least one year.

comments.name: She
comments.body:
If Trump cares about American interests, he would reach a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz immediately. 

Lifting sanctions and letting Iranians gain access to their own assets seems reasonable to me. Letting them officially control the Strait with Oman to assure the maintenance and security of the waterway is reasonable too, considering Panama has long charged fees and exercised control  since President Carter handed over the Panama Canal. The issue of nuclear enrichment can be dealt with separately, since Trump bombed out the possibility of any imminent threat more than a year ago, as he boasted back then.

Janet

comments.name: Marge Keller
comments.body:
"On a stairway between floors, I noticed a striking object mounted on a white wall. Bright red. Cylindrical. Industrial, but elegant. I stopped to look."

Well, I'm the first to admit that I tend to take fire extinguishers for granted . . .  until heaven forbid I may need one.

I read a book a few years ago about the horrific and tragic Our Lady of the Angels fire in a Chicago Catholic school on December 1, 1958 resulting in 95 deaths - 3 nuns and 92 children.  During the investigation of the fire, there were fire extinguishers in the hallways - but they were mounted on walls 7 feet from the ground.  When I read that sentence I thought "Good grief, even Michael Jordan wouldn't have been able to reach one to help put out a fire.

It was such a horrific tragedy.  The book is a difficult one to read but truly one worth the effort.

Fire terrifies me more than anything.  Always has.

I have a backyard filled with native species of flowers, trees, shrubs and grasses which I planted for the birds and pollinators and birds. I've also got a plum, pear and apple tree which I harvest from in good years but the squirrels get their share too. 

However, this past year there was a late Spring frost which froze the fruit tree blossoms so none of my fruit trees set fruit. I feel empathy for the squirrels. It is going to be a hard winter for them. I didn't even get raspberries and currants which are usually more reliable than the fruit trees in producing.

My question for Mr Greenfield is does he take into account that other species (birds, squirrels, chipmunks, fox, raccoons etc all native to Turtle Island) need the wild food he is sourcing from these parks? They need to eat too.

I hope he at least considers other species' needs on particularly poor harvest years. They don't have access to grocery stores.

comments.name: Lyle Ross

Something to consider.  The course I took in evolution still heavily referenced the hypothesis that all mutations were random.  Then, natural selection brought those which gave an advatage to the surface, they persisted.

A lizard, with shorter legs, would have an advatage over one with long legs, in a narrow environment.  Repeated mutations resulting in shorter and shorter limbs would allow offspring access to tighter and tighter spaces and new food sources or possibly, better hiding places.

Alternatively, a sloth that poops on its own tree is more likely to get said poop on its food and suffer disease.  One, that for some reason had a predilection to poop on the forest floor would be healthier and pass on more offspring.  That would allow natural selection to give its offspring an advantage.

Deer antlers don't just maintain injury status,  they are an imprinted pattern.  The antlers grow in the same pattern every year, adding a new point each season.  That pattern gives the deer an advantage in mating.  An older buck has bigger antlers and can fight to pass on genes.  Evolution doesn't give the best solution, just a solution.  The biological tool that tracks antler growth with age might be based on the previous year's growth pattern and would thus communicate injuries.

For fun.  Male and female reindeer both have antlers.   Males get them during breeding season.  Females get them prior to giving birth, presumably to protect their young.

Some display trivia: 

(1) Development of light-emitting diodes (LEDs) started in the 1930s (they are commonly used as backlights for LCD monitors and televisions today).

(2) Liquid-crystal displays only pass about 5% of the light from their illumination sources. The rest (95%) is absorbed in polarizing filters, color filters, and other glass surfaces. 

(3) LCD panels for monitors and televisions have become so inexpensive to manufacture that most companies have stopped making them except in China - the profit margins are low. A 65-inch 4K LCD panel has a wholesale price under $100 now.

(4) The display market is slowly moving away from LCDs to direct-view displays using arrays of thousands of tiny LEDs (micro LED). You can already buy televisions with this technology - it's not cheap, but will become so over time with economies of scale. And the LED manufacturing business is largely concentrated in (where else?) China.

(5) The other competing technology, organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) have been in development since the 1960s. The current technology, white OLEDs with color filters, was discovered by accident by two Eastman Kodak engineers in the 1980s and has been licensed to LG Electronics. OLEDs aren't as bright as LEDs, but do not have as many layers to manufacture and work well in small electronics (watches, phones. tablets, etc.)

I do believe that it is more acceptable to play media from your phone if it is quiet and/or you are away from others, but just investing in a pair of headphones is a win-win as it not only completely eliminates the disturbance but also lets you play your music/videos louder.  There is no way to expect what type of sounds will play from someone’s phone until it happens. While one might argue that public places are meant to be loud anyway, playing videos or music in public is more sharp than normal background noise such as cars driving or people talking. There is a different level of annoyance here as playing something from your phone often pierces through the blend of background noise and is distinctly audible for those around you. From Swansea, Wales, yet disappointingly not a single word about that brilliant conflicted poet writer Dylan Thomas, who was also from Swansea - "that ugly, little town" - and had made the U.S. a second home like Ms Zeta-Jones. Thomas's late daughter, Aeronwy, also hailed from Swansea but tragically passed away too young not long ago from an undiagnosed illness, a fate that easily befalls struggling artists - unlike the more fortunate Ms Zeta-Jones. I had the privilege of meeting and assisting Aeronwy and Welsh scholar poet Peter Thabit Jones, on their first U.S. tour hosted by Cross Cultural Communications.

"Do not go gentle into that good night," and "And death shall have no dominion", the "play for voices" Under Milk Wood, are just some of Thomas's great works readers are familiar with.

People can go to Laugharne to see Dylan Thomas's family home and the Boathouse - where he wrote many works - his grave and the splinidly simple grave marker.

Please, please, let's not forget significant Welsh underpinnings to contemporary literature and poetry. As we well know, literature in general, and the English language which also means the elegant beauty of the written word, are ever under assault and being destroyed by the gross distortions of this modern world. Sadly, that Dylan Thomas (nor his daughter) is not even noted in passing is yet another missed opportunity and case in point.

comments.name: J.D.

Brazil has a population of 200M+ yet in both its hotly contested 2022 and 2026 presidential elections the winner was determined 3–4 hours after polls closed.

France, Germany, Britain, Spain, Chile, Argentina, Mexico, and many other developed and developing countries regularly produce meaningful preliminary results on election night.

Surely we in the United States of America are capable of doing the same.

Understood that final certification can take longer, and exceptionally close races may require additional counting... but at what point do we stop treating these days- and weeks-long delays as unavoidable and start asking why we can't do what other countries do?

The argument that faster results compromise election security is unconvincing. If that were true, we'd have to assume that elections in all these other countries are inaccurate. I can understand concerns about election integrity in countries like Brazil or Mexico, given long-standing corruption problems, but does that argument really hold for every country that counts results faster than us?

Back in the days of the pony express, it took states significant time to count ballots, and then a significant amount of time to transport the results to Washington DC from say, California.

One of the express powers reserve to the states in the United States constitution is the right to prescribe the manner of conducting elections within its borders. States that accept ballots as long as they were mailed on or before election day, must include them in the final count.

I love poetry. I’ve subscribed to Poetry Magazine for 20+ years and I’m an unpublished amateur poet. 

That said, I know of no other field of literature, science, the humanities, etc that spends so much time trying to justify its existence and express how important it is. Poetry has a complex, and it may be deserved. 

The poetry sphere (in the US at least) is quite small, and instead of writing so persistently about how important poetry is, I’m wondering if the field could spend more time instead asking how to increase engagement across the age spectrum and socioeconomics, particularly in this age when social media is robbing society of so much of the humanities and much attention has moved to podcasts, audiobooks and the like. 

I read a good amount - prose and poetry - and the reality is that I only find about 5% of both genres interesting. That’s natural for most people I suspect and it might be an overestimate if there is data on such things. 

A lot of poetry is so arcane and takes so much effort to determine what’s being communicated that I don’t find it appealing, and when I think about my friends, it partly explains why the majority have little interest in poetry at all.

comments.name: I Am

We definitely are in this together and then some: Fundamental separation isn't findable from this perspective.

All suffering/dissatisfaction appearing is due to the conditioning associated with the assumption of fundamental separation, particularly between self and everything else.

Once there is an apparently separate "me" here and a world of "other" over there, there is something that must be protected, defended, completed, validated, compared, maintained, and controlled. What is appearing can then be divided into what "I" want and don't want, what should and shouldn't be happening, what threatens or benefits "me", and what must change before "I" can be okay. 

When conditioning associated with being a separate, isolated "me" dissolves, compassion appears naturally. This isn't because someone becomes better or special, but because the boundary between "me" and "others" disappears. When others are not experienced as fundamentally separate, their pain, joy, and vulnerability feel extremely intimate, more relatable, less abstract. Kindness and care don't need to be imposed as rules; they emerge as a sensible self-evident response to what's appearing. 

That doesn't mean compassion appears perfectly in every moment. Old habits, stress, fear, and conditioning may still appear. But when they do, they may pass, without self-judgment or justification. 

Our issues can't be solved using the same assumptions that got us to this point.
